title: Growing Artificial Societies: Social Science From the Bottom Up

key_points.claim: Foundational Sugarscape work: collective behaviors (group formation, culture, combat, trade) emerge from simple local agent rules.
key_points.evidence_quote: group formation, cultural transmission, combat, and trade are seen to “emerge” from the interaction of individual agents following simple local rules.

key_points.claim: Agent design: heterogeneous genetic attributes, a simple movement rule, and metabolism-driven death.
key_points.evidence_quote: Agents are born onto the Sugarscape with a vision, a metabolism, a speed, and other genetic attributes.

key_points.claim: Environment and wealth: seasons produce migration and hibernation, and resource accumulation yields a wealth distribution.
key_points.evidence_quote: when seasons are introduced, migration and hibernation can be observed. Agents are accumulating sugar at all times, so there is always a distribution of wealth.

key_points.claim: Culture and conflict: on a twin-peaked landscape, agents self-organize into culturally distinct tribes that fight and compete for cultural dominance.
key_points.evidence_quote: self-organization into spatially segregated and culturally distinct “tribes” centered on the peaks of the Sugarscape.

key_points.claim: Demography: sexual reproduction can lead to population crash or to ecological collapse from overpopulation.
key_points.evidence_quote: the population becomes thin, birth rates fall, and the population can crash.

key_points.claim: Economy: adding a second resource (spice) and trade produces an emergent market. Pollution from resource-mining allows study of markets with environmental factors.
key_points.evidence_quote: introduce a second resource (spice) to the Sugarscape and allow the agents to trade, an economic market emerges.

reliability_notes: Publisher's book description page only (a summary, not full text). It describes a 1996 classic and gives no state-of-the-art or recent findings. Treat as abstract only.
